# Chickagami Park, Geauga Park District | Venue - Burton, OH | Wedding Spot
### Description:
For those seeking a celebration immersed in nature look no further than Chickagami Park. This preserve consists of 139 acres of woods, wetlands, streams, and uplands. Enjoy an outdoor ceremony on the ground of Chickagami Park. The lush green environment creates an exciting as well as a beautifully picturesque scene to wed in. The Overlook Shelter is a good reception or ceremony venue for those who would like to celebrate outdoors. The view of the wetland meadow is stunning and a wonderful sight during the day that transforms to prime stargazing by night. The Pine Grove Shelter is a handsome facility for your wedding reception. Guests will be encouraged to let loose in this simple and inviting environment. Dine and dance well into the evening in this cool venue. Chickagami Park is an attractive and simple wedding venue that celebrates the pure joy of love, marriage, friendship, and family coming together for a special event.

Title: The Life and Fiery Death of the World's Biggest Treehouse
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,8,9,10,11
For the thousands of people around the world who’d once visited and admired the world’s largest treehouse in Crossville, Tennessee, the news came as an awful shock. In October 2019, [a blaze consumed the singular construction](https://www.crossville-chronicle.com/news/local_news/fire-destroys-ministers-treehouse/article_30c3ad96-f686-11e9-ade9-5b8bf1310272.html). But for Horace Burgess, the treehouse’s architect, this is just how things go. He was well acquainted with how it feels to lose your own, self-built treehouse in an angry conflagration. Heck, he’d already burned one down himself.
“It was just evil,” says Burgess of the older treehouse he built and then razed back in the 1980s. There was “no good about it.” The house had ended up serving as Burgess’s hideaway for doing drugs, which he committed to quitting after the deaths of some friends. Trouble was, the house itself had become part of the habit. A voice came to Burgess, saying that he had to burn the house down if he was going to rebuild his life. And it wasn’t just any voice.
People typically think “you’re a little bit crazy when you say that God spoke to you,” Burgess admits, “but really he’s the one that tells us to put our pants on in the morning.” Looking back, Burgess says that burning that first treehouse down—on God’s advice—was “probably the most sane moment in my life.”

![Image 1: The fire that claimed the singular construction. ](https://img.atlasobscura.com/Ho7pQXcjdpu5AhR27V8MoffutibdPPvJUwabD3maGeQ/rt:fill/w:1200/el:1/q:81/sm:1/scp:1/ar:1/aHR0cHM6Ly9hdGxh/cy1kZXYuczMuYW1h/em9uYXdzLmNvbS91/cGxvYWRzL2Fzc2V0/cy82ODQxMDg4ZmUz/NjYzMzcyYThfU2Ny/ZWVuIFNob3QgMjAy/MC0wNC0xNyBhdCAy/LjM5LjQ0IFBNLnBu/Zw.png)
The fire that claimed the singular construction. [Courtesy Crossville Chronicle](https://www.crossville-chronicle.com/news/local_news/fire-destroys-ministers-treehouse/article_30c3ad96-f686-11e9-ade9-5b8bf1310272.html)
Having freed himself from the demons trapped in that treehouse, Burgess, a pastor who grew up in Crossville, set about dedicating his life to religion and his community. Ironically, those commitments quickly brought him right back to building treehouses. After all, he knew he could do it well, and he understood that if he could share it with others it could serve as a positive force in the community rather than as a destructive force in his private life. “It was just something I enjoyed doing,” he says, seemingly uninterested in understanding why. As an aside, he mentions casually that he’d actually completed five or six treehouses in total by that point in time—even if people only ever seem to talk about the one that was about to come.

So, in 1993, Burgess got down to work on his family’s farm—139 acres that, according to Burgess, once contained a “zoo” with two of each animal, like a landlocked Noah’s Ark in central Tennessee. Not knowing where things would lead, he simply started by building a staircase, one he actually called the “Stairway to Nowhere.” It was more meditative than anything else. “I had totally turned my life over to the lord,” he says, and inspiration struck one day when he was actually “sitting down and praying for anything but a treehouse.” It was then that “the Spirit of God quickened me,” he says, and Horace Burgess gave in to the treehouse impulse and resolved to turn the Stairway to Nowhere into the world’s largest arboreal construct. And why not the largest? God had promised Burgess, after all, that he would never run out of material as long as he kept building, and building, and building. It sounds Old Testament stuff.

[Pete Nelson](https://www.nelsontreehouse.com/)—a professional treehouse architect who has built more than 350 over the course of his career, and who hosts the show _Treehouse Masters_ on Animal Planet—was similarly impressed. “As a builder,” says Nelson, “I was just really intrigued by how he managed to take what were clearly just leftover scraps and turn them into this edifice.” With first-hand knowledge of what goes into creating “something like that, and knowing it was just him,” all Nelson could say was, “Wow, this guy is the real deal.” Indeed, Nelson returned years later with a camera crew to shoot an episode of _Treehouse Masters_ about Burgess’s creation.
![Image 5: People typically think “you’re a little bit crazy when you say that God spoke to you, but really he’s the one that tells us to put our pants on in the morning.” ](https://img.atlasobscura.com/EQO92bQYOxrDlM8yTR-Lv5iNxCFz34gqG381pNtxWOQ/rt:fill/w:1200/el:1/q:81/sm:1/scp:1/ar:1/aHR0cHM6Ly9hdGxh/cy1kZXYuczMuYW1h/em9uYXdzLmNvbS91/cGxvYWRzL2Fzc2V0/cy81YzUwMTNjNTkw/ZmI5MGVlNzdfX21n/XzI3MzZfMTgyMjc3/NjQ1MjNfby5qcGc.jpg)
People typically think “you’re a little bit crazy when you say that God spoke to you, but really he’s the one that tells us to put our pants on in the morning.” [Courtesy Lindsey Turner](https://www.flickr.com/photos/theogeo/albums/72157654212523300/with/18225603154/)

And so, for years, Horace Burgess played the humble carnival barker, welcoming strangers into his mystical offroad apparition. That changed in 2012, when the authorities permanently shut down visits over safety concerns. According to Burgess, a retired engineer who had come by the treehouse wrote to the state that he “had seen some things that was unsafe,” leading to an inspection that resulted in the declaration of a public hazard. The state, says Burgess, wanted him to pay for new engineering work to be done to bring the treehouse up to code. Burgess wasn’t interested.
“Everything in it was unsafe,” Burgess admits with a laugh. “I see no way that you could make a 97-foot treehouse safe,” at least not in the legal sense. While no visitors had ever been hurt, Burgess didn’t fight the decision—just as he had done before, he simply let it go. He sold the property and returned to private life, his massive creation looming just down the road in majestic obsolescence.
Glenn Clark, the most recent owner of the property, told [local television station WBIR](https://www.wbir.com/article/news/local/famous-ministers-treehouse-in-crossville-suddenly-burns-to-the-ground/51-58e7b861-8244-48cb-b632-d828ec925b2c) that he had no intention of tearing the treehouse down, had no idea what caused the fire, and was upset about its destruction. Clark could’t be reached for comment.

## A daily dose of hidden gems to visit, extraordinary places to eat  and wondrous stories from around the world.
![Image 6: The last treehouse was Burgess's largest one, but several had come before. ](https://img.atlasobscura.com/suDkhOObF8NImdPbU4dfUWRALIZSRjMdEQGDsgxi0K4/rt:fill/w:1200/el:1/q:81/sm:1/scp:1/ar:1/aHR0cHM6Ly9hdGxh/cy1kZXYuczMuYW1h/em9uYXdzLmNvbS91/cGxvYWRzL2Fzc2V0/cy9lMjVjZDg1ZmM2/MzY1NGM5YmVfTW9z/YWljIDIgY29weS5w/bmc.png)
The last treehouse was Burgess’s largest one, but several had come before. [Courtesy Lindsey Turner](https://www.flickr.com/photos/theogeo/albums/72157654212523300/with/18225603154/)
* * *
Not everyone, however, was willing to let it go. Lindsey Turner, a graphic designer from western Tennessee, visited the treehouse years after it was formally closed, and trespassed onto the property in 2015. “I just love strange, relatively little-known, off places,” she says, likening the treehouse’s spirit to that of the [“Mindfield”](https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/billy-tripps-mindfield) in Brownsville, Tennessee, a kind of physical diary documenting the life of the artist, Billy Tripp. The treehouse, she says, was “a living piece of art that was constantly changing. I just thought that’s something I’ve got to try to see”—even if that meant getting loose with the law.

## A daily dose of hidden gems to visit, extraordinary places to eat  and wondrous stories from around the world.
She braved the condemned public hazard on her own, and wrote in a [blog post](http://theogeo.com/blog/tennessee/climbing-up-the-ministers-treehouse/) that “I felt my stomach jump up to my throat as I thought about how I was two, three, four, five floors up on wooden boards that were constructed by a man with no blueprints”—a sensation not exactly quelled by the “widely spaced floor boards” that allowed her to look down and see just how high she had climbed. Still, in yet another nod to Burgess’s amateur architectural prowess, she says it all felt “surprisingly stable.”
The musician [Lilly Hiatt](https://www.lillyhiatt.com/), who visited the treehouse just in summer 2019, felt safe for reasons beyond the building’s structural integrity. She understood that Burgess “had so much thoughtfulness in his heart when he was making this,” and she could feel that. She “felt very comforted,” she says, “by the inspiration of it all,” adding that the feeling she had in the house was more intense than any she’s gotten inside a traditional church. “It felt very loving,” she says, and in turn she “didn’t feel too guilty about the trespassing.” It was clear from standing inside that Burgess “built this because he wanted people to see it and feel inspired by it, and that’s what I came here to do.” If she were caught, she figured, “maybe he’ll pardon me.”

![Image 1: Tennessee Was Once Home to the World’s Largest Treehouse](https://townsquare.media/site/76/files/2024/01/attachment-Untitled-design-94-1.jpg?w=980&q=75)
One of my favorite things to do when I was a kid was hang out in a neighbor friend's treehouse. Actually, it was a complex of treehouses; there were three trees and you could go back and forth between all of them.
Then there was the Swiss Family Robinson Treehouse at Disney World, an attraction that closed years ago. The idea of maximizing space like that and making it livable fascinated me. No it was not an exciting attraction, but it was one we never missed.

### Tennessee Once Laid Claim to the World's Largest Treehouse
My admiration for all that goes into constructing a good treehouse was the main reason I was attracted to a Facebook post about a creepy but beautiful old abandoned treehouse in Crossville TN. It was, as it turns out, the world's largest.
And I'm not exactly sure treeHOUSE is the right word. That thing looks more like a tree HOTEL. It was called the Minister's Treehouse because, well, it was built by a minister. His name is Horace Burgess and he got started on it in the early 90s. It began with 80 rooms before Burgess began adding to it. And it became such a high-profile endeavor that lumber donations started coming in.

### The World's Largest Treehouse Welcomed All Visitors
Built as what I might call a monument to God, based on the prayers Burgess said regarding the project, the 97-foot tall structure was naturally an attractive destination for sightseers. Seriously. "Welcome" and "no smoking" were the only signs on the treehouse. Anyone could visit...until 2012, [according to Travel and Leisure](https://www.travelandleisure.com/travel-news/crossville-tennessee-famous-worlds-tallest-treehouse-burns-down#:~:text=It%20was%20open%20to%20the,coming%20to%20see%20it%20unofficially.):
It was open to the public for anyone to visit for free. However the Tennessee State Fire Marshall shut down the tree house in 2012. It had become overrun with tourists and was labeled a fire safety hazard because it didn’t have sprinklers or a fire alarm. But that didn’t stop people from coming to see it unofficially.

### Sadly, the World's Largest Treehouse Is No Longer With Us
But people no longer come to see it unofficially. You might have noticed that I said the treehouse WAS the world's largest. That's because, sadly, it burned to the ground in 2019.
It's interesting. While I mildly mourn the loss of such an unusual landmark, I'm simultaneously amused by its creator's take on the fire. After it burned, Burgess [told the New York Times,](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/26/us/tennessee-treehouse-fire.html) "It's always been a pain."
But hey, treehouse aficionados, not to worry. T[he world's largest treehouse RESORT is also located in Tennessee](https://www.travelandleisure.com/hotels-resorts/vacation-rentals/worlds-largest-tree-house-resort-great-smoky-national-park). You'll just have to drive a little farther down Interstate 40.

## History and description
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Burgess%27s_Treehouse&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and description")]
[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Horace_Burgess_Treehouse_Aug._27%2C_2011.jpg/250px-Horace_Burgess_Treehouse_Aug._27%2C_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Horace_Burgess_Treehouse_Aug._27,_2011.jpg)
The exterior of the treehouse

## History and description
Horace Burgess, a local minister, was praying in 1993 when he said God told him, "If you build a tree house, I'll see that you never run out of material."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-slate2013-1) Inspired by the vision, Burgess began building the treehouse and continued working on it for the next 12 years.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) The 97-foot-tall (30 m) tree house and church was supported by a still-living 80 ft (24 m)[white oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_oak "White oak") tree with a 12 ft-diameter (3.7 m) base, and relied on six other oak trees for support.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-usa2007-5) He built it using 258,000 nails with a nailgun, and about 500 pounds of penny nails driven by hand.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) The treehouse was located on Beehive Lane in [Crossville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee "Crossville, Tennessee").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-6)

## History and description
Over time, Burgess' treehouse became a popular tourist attraction.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyd2012-7) Burgess officiated 23 weddings in the treehouse church,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) and when not in service, the sanctuary doubled as a basketball court.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-independent2009-8) Although there is no [Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records") category for largest treehouse, it was often referred to as the world's largest.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-hp2012-9)[Pete Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Nelson "Pete Nelson"), the host of _[Treehouse Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treehouse\_Masters "Treehouse Masters")_ on [Animal Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_Planet "Animal Planet"), who has written six books about treehouses and owns a business building them, said it was "by far" the largest in the world.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3)

## History and description
In August 2012, the structure was closed to public access by the state because it had become a public attraction but did not follow building and fire safety codes.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-10)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-hazzard-2) It was a "deathtrap", said one official, "it was very cool, but also very dangerous."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-Jones-4) The structure stood vacant and dilapidated for years, becoming a frequent target of vandalism.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-fire-11) On October 22, 2019, the treehouse and its supporting trees completely burned to the ground in an inferno lasting about 15 minutes.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-12) The fire department responded; however, by the time they arrived nothing was left to save.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-fire-11) "It was basically a pile of rubble when we pulled up. The fire was so intense we had to park 500 yards away", said an official.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-Jones-4) Fire officials said there was no electricity on site and no electric storms. The recent new owner of the treehouse, who had no insurance, declined to open an investigation.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) Burgess said most of the marriages he officiated there had not lasted, and that he was relieved after the fire; the treehouse had "always been a pain" he said.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3)
*   [The Big Treehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Big_Treehouse "The Big Treehouse")

Title: Historyfeels on Instagram: "Horace Burgess’s “Minister’s Treehouse” in Crossville, Tennessee. Beginning in 1993, Burgess, who said God spoke to him to build it, spent twelve years building a towering, 97‑foot‑tall wooden cathedral among live oak and pine trees.

The sprawling structure, often called the world’s largest treehouse, spread over five stories and 80 rooms, including classrooms, bedrooms, a kitchen, and multiple decks.

A spiral staircase linked its maze-like interior, which featured a sanctuary with pews and choir loft, a miniature basketball court, and even a belfry of oxygen‑acetylene canisters as bells. 

Burgess officiated 23 weddings within its walls, and up to 1,000 visitors per week came to marvel at this wooden wonder.

Shut down in 2012 for failing fire-code regulations, the treehouse sat abandoned for years before being engulfed in a devastating blaze on October 22, 2019. Fire crews arrived to find only rubble, the inferno reportedly collapsing the entire structure in under 15 minutes"

In August 2012, the structure was closed to public access by the state because it had become a public attraction but did not follow building and fire safety codes.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-10)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-hazzard-2) It was a "deathtrap", said one official, "it was very cool, but also very dangerous."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-Jones-4) The structure stood vacant and dilapidated for years, becoming a frequent target of vandalism.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-fire-11) On October 22, 2019, the treehouse and its supporting trees completely burned to the ground in an inferno lasting about 15 minutes.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-12) The fire department responded; however, by the time they arrived nothing was left to save.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-fire-11) "It was basically a pile of rubble when we pulled up. The fire was so intense we had to park 500 yards away", said an official.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-Jones-4) Fire officials said there was no electricity on site and no electric storms. The recent new owner of the treehouse, who had no insurance, declined to open an investigation.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) Burgess said most of the marriages he officiated there had not lasted, and that he was relieved after the fire; the treehouse had "always been a pain" he said.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3)

Horace Burgess’s “Minister’s Treehouse” in Crossville, Tennessee. Beginning in 1993, Burgess, who said God spoke to him to build it, spent twelve years building a towering, 97‑foot‑tall wooden cathedral among live oak and pine trees.  
The sprawling structure, often called the world’s largest treehouse, spread over five stories and 80 rooms, including classrooms, bedrooms, a kitchen, and multiple decks.
A spiral staircase linked its maze-like interior, which featured a sanctuary with pews and choir loft, a miniature basketball court, and even a belfry of oxygen‑acetylene canisters as bells.
texts.3:
Burgess officiated 23 weddings within its walls, and up to 1,000 visitors per week came to marvel at this wooden wonder.
Shut down in 2012 for failing fire-code regulations, the treehouse sat abandoned for years before being engulfed in a devastating blaze on October 22, 2019. Fire crews arrived to find only rubble, the inferno reportedly collapsing the entire structure in under 15 minutes
